sections.title: Synopsis
paragraphs: Mostly dry conditions this afternoon as brief ridging moves through the area. sections.title: Short term (tonight through Wednesday night)
paragraphs: Drier conditions this evening with post frontal showers mainly offshore. With some light surface gradients tonight into Tuesday morning, will likely see areas of fog early Tuesday AM, for areas in the Southwest Interior and Central Puget Sound. Onshore flow in the afternoon will help the fog dissipate with high temperatures generally in the low 50s for most areas.

A upper level trough offshore will start to dig southwards Tuesday into Wednesday. This system will primarily move south of our area but will rotate showers over the southern half of the area, additionally along the coast on Wednesday. Along with precipitation, easterly winds will kick up slightly, especially in the Cascade gaps, with probabilities of gusts over 35 MPH generally around 40-60% across much of the gaps Wednesday morning. High temps will be slightly cooler with upper 40s and low 50s, areas along the Southwest Interior and coast could see highs in the mid 40s. Overnight lows in the low to mid 30s.

sections.title: Long term (Thursday through Monday)
paragraphs: Drier conditions Thursday into Friday as the aforementioned low rotates southward away from western Washington. Likely will see areas of fog Friday morning as residual moisture remains. Upper level troughing and a upper level low will drop down from the Gulf of Alaska and will situate itself over the coast into the weekend. Light precipitation comes back into the forecast over the weekend as the low spins showers up in the area. Latest ensemble guidance suggests a more active, wetter pattern through the first half of the week with multiple systems entering the area.
Mazurkiewicz

sections.title: Aviation
paragraphs: Conditions are predominantly VFR tonight, though isolated MVFR cigs will remain possible for terminals along the coast (KHQM) this evening as showers continue to move inland across the Olympic Peninsula. With conditions clearing across the interior, fog is expected to develop overnight into Tuesday morning, first across the South Sound and Chehalis River Valley (impacting KOLM), then later spreading into other portions of Puget Sound and resulting in the potential for conditions to deteriorate to IFR/LIFR for a few hours early Tuesday morning. Conditions will then rebound to VFR by mid-morning as fog dissipates.

KSEA...VFR conditions will continue tonight with southerly winds persisting at 3-6 kt. Areas of fog look to develop overnight into Tuesday morning and could encroach upon the terminal. As a result, conditions may drop down to IFR for a few hours on Tuesday morning, with latest probabilistic guidance hinting at about a 10% chance of IFR conditions developing between 12-14Z.

sections.title: Marine
paragraphs: Seas across the coastal waters this evening are still hovering between 14-16 ft but will continue to subside towards 10-12 ft by Tuesday morning. Overall, winds remain much lighter across the area waters today due to high pressure which has built back into the region. Winds will increase through the day on Tuesday and will turn offshore by Tuesday night as a low pressure system offshore moves southward through the NE Pacific. Winds will be locally enhanced along the gaps in terrain, most notably through the Strait of Juan de Fuca and near Grays Harbor Tuesday night. Latest REFS guidance shows a 70-90% chance of wind gusts exceeding gale force across the outer coastal waters, so have have gone ahead and issued gale warnings for these areas. Gusts may also briefly reach gale along the inner coastal waters (especially the waters adjacent to the West Entrance of the Strait and along Grays Harbor County) but are not expected to be as long- lived. Nonetheless, additional small craft advisories are likely for the central and western Strait as easterly winds increase to 25-30 kt Tuesday night, as well for the inner coastal water zones on Tuesday as both winds and seas increase. Seas will build back to 12-15 ft Tuesday night into early Wednesday.

Calmer conditions will follow on Wednesday as the low pushes out of the area and then persist through Friday as high pressure builds back into the coastal waters in its wake. The pattern will become more active again heading into the weekend as another series of systems look to move through the area.

sections.title: Hydrology
paragraphs: The Skokomish River has fallen below flood stage and will continue to recede throughout the week. River flooding is not expected over the next several days, but chances increase again early next week (mostly on the Skokomish River) as the pattern becomes more active and additional rainfall is expected over the weekend and into early next week.

discussions.name: NWS Portland
synopsis: Scattered showers continue today while a high surf threat linger at the coast through this evening. After a temporary return to dry weather on Tuesday, another system undercutting the region to the south pushes precipitation into the area late Tuesday into Wednesday coupled with marginal snowfall concerns for the Cascade passes. Dry weather and areas of morning fog return again Thursday into Friday. Active weather likely returns this weekend, though impacts appear to remain relatively minimal.

sections.title: Discussion
paragraphs: Now through Sunday...Scattered showers continue this afternoon but should come to and end tonight as the axis of an upper level trough passes overhead. Dry conditions are then expected through at least Tuesday afternoon as transient ridge of high pressure briefly passes over the region. Areas of valley fog likely make a return with pockets of low visibility possible for those commuting in portions of the Willamette Valley and coastal valleys Tuesday morning.

The next weather system will approach Tuesday night into Wednesday as a surface low pressure system quickly spins up offshore. Model guidance shows a frontal boundary being ejected toward the Oregon coast before weakening as it lifts across the forecast area on Wednesday. The low pressure system will dive south as it slingshots toward California. This will likely minimize any impacts across the area with heaviest rainfall expected along the central Oregon coast and points farther south. Snow is also expected for the Cascades as snow levels are forecast to be around 3000-4000 ft Tue night into Wednesday. But chances for accumulations of 3" or more at Cascade pass level are low, at around 15-25%, during the 24-hour period. Will also mention there is around a 10% chance that snow levels fall to around 1500 ft in the central Columbia River Gorge and Upper Hood River where a few snow flurries may occur at elevation near Parkdale. Offshore easterly winds are also expected to increase Tuesday night as pressure gradients tighten in response to the low pressure offshore. East winds will likely be strongest through the Columbia River Gorge into the eastern Portland Metro area with gusts approaching 25-35 mph, locally higher near Corbett and at other typical windy spots. Meso-lows may also develop along the frontal boundary early late Tue/early Wed, but are expected to remain offshore as they lift north and west.

Ensembles remain in good agreement for another extended dry period Thursday into Friday as we see a brief break between systems. With higher pressure moving overhead Friday, light winds, and ample surface moisture, morning valley fog likely returns. Uncertainty increases late Friday night into the weekend as the progressive weather pattern returns increasing chances for low pressure systems to develop offshore, and over 70% of the 12z EPS members show precipitation returning by Saturday. A map of ensemble MSLP locations shows some uncertainty with the low placement but suggests it likely remains off the OR/WA coast instead of dropping south, which would maintain showery weather through Sunday. At this time any weather related impacts look to remain minimal. /DH

sections.title: Aviation
paragraphs: Through 06Z Wednesday...Chances for MVFR ceilings and pockets of IFR/LIFR fog and/or low stratus development increase tonight. KHIO, KUAO and KEUG have the highest probabilities for fog and/or low stratus development, however confidence is too low at KUAO and KEUG to include a mention of fog. Confidence is relatively higher at KHIO, and a mention of fog was included in the 06Z TAF package as the probability for surface visibilities less than 1 SM are around 50% between 11-17Z Tuesday. Regardless of which TAF sites experience fog and/or low stratus tonight, expect improvement to VFR by 18-21Z Tuesday as skies become mostly clear. High clouds increase from southwest to northeast between 03-06Z Wednesday ahead of the next frontal system. This system will bring rain back into the area, however rain is expected to hold off until after 06Z Wednesday.
Expect light and variable winds less than 5 kt through 18Z Tuesday. Offshore winds begin to increase a bit towards 04-06Z Wednesday ahead of the aforementioned frontal system.

KPDX AND APPROACHES...Predominately VFR conditions are expected through 10-12Z Tuesday, aside from brief ceiling drops to MVFR thresholds. Chances for ceilings below 3500 ft peak between 12-17Z Tuesday at 40-70%. -23

sections.title: Marine
paragraphs: Buoy observations continued to showed steep and hazardous seas over the central and southern waters with significant wave heights as high as 15 to 20 ft at 15 to 16 seconds. Wave heights over the northern waters have decreased to 12 to 17 ft at 15 to 16 seconds, with the highest wave heights beyond 20 NM offshore. Given wave heights have been falling more slowly over the central and southern waters, the Hazardous Seas Warning has been extended through 1 AM PST Tuesday for these marine zones. Hazardous Seas Warnings over the northern waters expired at 10 PM PST Monday and are no longer in effect. Wave heights will continue to gradually decrease tonight into Tuesday morning to around 10-12 ft for all marine zones. However, conditions will still be hazardous for small craft.

In addition, winds and seas will ramp back up Tuesday afternoon through Tuesday night as the next frontal system moves over the coastal waters, bringing southerly wind gusts up to 40 kt over the outer waters, with the highest gusts expected beyond 30 NM offshore. The inner waters will see relatively weaker winds from this incoming system, with gusts up to 30 kt. Therefore, Gale Warnings remain in effect for the outer waters Tuesday afternoon through Tuesday night. Winds weaken Wednesday, but with seas remaining elevated around 12-16 ft at 14 seconds due to a fresh westerly swell. Calmer conditions arrive on Thursday with seas falling below 10 ft and relatively light offshore winds. However, conditions look to ramp up once again this weekend as another system moves towards the coast, bringing southerly winds with gusts up to 30 kt and seas building towards 14-16 ft. -23/42
